areas.summary: GitLab CI and GitHub Actions pipelines: stages, gates, secrets, and artifact supply chain.

rules.name: pipeline-standards
rules.description: Stage order, gates, job settings, and secret handling for GitLab CI and GitHub Actions pipelines.
rules.body:
## Stages and gates

- Keep the stage order `lint` → `test` → `build` → `scan` → `deploy-staging` → `smoke-test` → `deploy-production`.
- Fail the `lint` job on any linter or format error; do not set `allow_failure: true` on lint, test, or scan jobs.
- Block the merge when any unit or integration test fails; keep line coverage of critical paths at 80 % or more.
- Fail the `scan` stage on any Critical or High finding of SAST, dependency, image, or secret scans.
- Tag every built image with the commit SHA (`$CI_COMMIT_SHA`, `${{ github.sha }}`); never push `latest`, `main`, or branch-name tags.
- Deploy to staging automatically after a merge to the default branch, then run the smoke test job against staging.
- Gate the `deploy-production` job with a protected environment and a manual approval; require staging to be healthy for 15 minutes first.
- Set `timeout:` (GitLab) or `timeout-minutes:` (GitHub) on every job.

## GitLab CI

- Use `rules:` for job conditions; do not use `only:` or `except:`.
- Split large pipelines with `include:` templates; keep shared templates in `.gitlab/ci/` or a template project pinned by `ref:`.
- Pin every job `image:` to a version tag or `@sha256` digest; never use `:latest`.
- Use `needs:` to build a DAG instead of waiting for whole stages.
- Set `cache:key:files:` on the lockfile for dependency caches and pass build outputs with `artifacts:` plus `expire_in:`.
- Store credentials in CI/CD variables marked `masked` and `protected`; never write a secret value in `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- Use `id_tokens:` for cloud and Vault authentication instead of static access keys.
- Run production deploy jobs only on protected branches or tags and with `environment:` set.

## GitHub Actions

- Set a top-level `permissions:` block with `contents: read` and add wider scopes per job only.
- Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA; keep the version in a trailing comment.
- Use `id-token: write` with OIDC (`aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`, `google-github-actions/auth`) instead of long-lived cloud keys.
- Read credentials only from `secrets.*` or environment secrets; never echo a secret or dump `env` in a step.
- Use reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) for steps shared across repositories.
- Use GitHub Environments with required reviewers for the production deploy job.
- Add `.github/dependabot.yml` for `github-actions` and the package ecosystem of the repository.

## Pipeline as code

- Keep all pipeline configuration in the repository; do not configure jobs in the CI web UI.
- Run deploy jobs on ephemeral runners without privileged mode unless the job file documents the reason.
- Never store cloud credentials or a kubeconfig on the runner disk after the job ends.

rules.name: supply-chain-security
rules.description: Signing, provenance, SBOM, and pinning requirements for artifacts that a pipeline builds and deploys.
rules.body:
- Sign every release image keylessly with `cosign sign --yes <image>@sha256:<digest>` from the CI job identity.
- Verify signatures in the deploy job with `cosign verify --certificate-oidc-issuer` and `--certificate-identity-regexp` bound to the repository and release refs.
- Keep signing keys in a KMS or HSM and rotate them at least every 90 days when keyless signing is not available.
- Generate an SLSA provenance attestation for every production build and bind it to the commit SHA.
- Generate a CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM for the exact image digest and store it with the artifact.
- Deploy images by `@sha256` digest only; never reference `latest` or another mutable tag in a manifest.
- Pin base images in every `Dockerfile` by `@sha256` digest.
- Commit lockfiles (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, `go.sum`, `gradle.lockfile`) for every direct dependency set.
- Enable checksum verification of the package manager (`npm ci`, `pip install --require-hashes`, `GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly`).
- Pin CI includes, actions, and plugins to an immutable commit SHA or tag `ref:`.
- Fail the deploy job when signature, provenance, or SBOM verification fails or the verifier is unreachable.
- Limit a policy exception to 14 days and record its owner and expiry date in the policy file.
- Keep commit SHA, SBOM digest, provenance digest, signer identity, and scan results for each release for at least 1 year.

skills.name: github-actions-patterns
skills.description: Procedure to add or change a GitHub Actions workflow: pin actions, set token permissions, cache, reuse workflows, and debug a failed run. Use when you edit files under .github/workflows/.
skills.body:
## 1. Read the current workflows

1. List `.github/workflows/*.yml` and the `on:` triggers of each file.
2. Find reusable workflows (`on: workflow_call`) and composite actions under `.github/actions/`.
3. Change the reusable workflow only when the task says so; otherwise change the caller.

## 2. Make the change

1. Set `permissions:` at the top of the workflow to the minimum, for example `contents: read`. Grant more per
   job only where a step needs it.
2. Pin every third-party action to a full commit SHA and keep the version in a comment:
   `uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha> # v4.2.2`.
3. Use `actions/setup-python`, `actions/setup-go`, or `actions/setup-java` with their built-in `cache:` input
   before you add a separate `actions/cache` step.
4. Set `timeout-minutes:` on every job.
5. Add `concurrency:` with `cancel-in-progress: true` for pull request workflows.
6. Move steps that two workflows share into a reusable workflow or a composite action.
7. Use `pull_request`, not `pull_request_target`, for code from forks. If `pull_request_target` is required, do
   not check out the fork head in that job.
8. Do not put `${{ github.event.* }}` text such as titles or branch names directly into `run:`; pass it through
   `env:` and quote the variable.
9. Read cloud credentials with OIDC (`permissions: id-token: write`) instead of long-lived secrets.
10. Put deploys behind a GitHub Environment with required reviewers. Ask the user first before you trigger a
    production deploy.

## 3. Validate before you push

```bash
actionlint                      # syntax, expressions, shellcheck of run: blocks
zizmor .github/workflows/       # security findings (optional)
```

If `actionlint` is not installed, run it as a container: `docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/repo -w /repo rhysd/actionlint`.

## 4. Debug a failed run

1. Get the log: `gh run list --limit 5`, then `gh run view <run-id> --log-failed`.
2. Find the first failing step and its first error line.
3. Decide the cause class:
   - **Permissions** — a `403` or `Resource not accessible by integration` needs a `permissions:` entry.
   - **Secret missing** — secrets are empty in workflows from forks and in environments that do not define them.
   - **Cache** — check the cache key inputs; a changed lock file must change the key.
   - **Runner image** — compare the tool versions with the last green run.
4. Rerun failed jobs with debug logs once: `gh run rerun <run-id> --failed --debug`.
5. Fix the cause and push. Do not add `continue-on-error: true` to make the run green.

## 5. Done

- `actionlint` passes and the workflow run on the branch is green.
- No action is referenced by a tag or a branch.

skills.name: gitlab-ci-patterns
skills.description: Procedure to add or change a GitLab CI pipeline: validate .gitlab-ci.yml, structure jobs with rules/needs/include, cache, and debug a failed job. Use when you edit .gitlab-ci.yml or files under .gitlab/ci/.
skills.body:
## 1. Read the current pipeline

1. Open `.gitlab-ci.yml` and every file it pulls in with `include:` (`local`, `project`, `template`, `component`).
2. List the stages, the jobs per stage, and which jobs run on merge requests, on the default branch, and on tags.
3. If the project uses CI components or a shared template project, change the caller first. Change the shared
   template only when the task says so.

## 2. Make the change

1. Put job conditions in `rules:`. Do not add `only:` or `except:`.
2. Express job order with `needs:` when a job does not need the whole previous stage.
3. Reuse setup with `extends:` or `!reference`; do not copy a `script:` block into a second job.
4. Pin every `image:` to a version tag or a digest. Do not use `latest`.
5. Set `timeout:` on jobs that can hang (integration tests, deploys).
6. Set `interruptible: true` on test jobs so a new push cancels the old pipeline.
7. Cache dependencies with a key that changes with the lock file:

```yaml
cache:
  key:
    files: [poetry.lock]   # go.sum, pom.xml, package-lock.json
  paths: [.venv/]
  policy: pull-push        # use `pull` in jobs that only read the cache
```

8. Pass build outputs with `artifacts:` and an `expire_in:` value. Use `artifacts:reports:junit` for test results.
9. Read secrets from CI/CD variables (masked and protected) or from `id_tokens:` with OIDC. Never write a secret
   into the YAML.
10. Put deploy jobs on `environment:` with `rules:` that limit them to protected branches or tags. A production
    deploy job uses `when: manual`; ask the user first before you run it.

## 3. Validate before you push

1. Lint the file with the API or the CLI:

```bash
glab ci lint                       # uses the project CI lint endpoint
glab ci lint --dry-run --ref main  # simulate a pipeline on a branch
```

2. If `glab` is not available, open CI/CD > Editor > Validate in the project UI.
3. Check that each changed job has the expected `rules:` outcome on a merge request and on the default branch.

## 4. Debug a failed job

1. Get the log: `glab ci view` or `glab ci trace <job-id>`.
2. Find the first error line, not the last one.
3. Decide the cause class:
   - **Script error** — reproduce locally with the same image: `docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/w -w /w <image> sh`.
   - **Missing variable** — check that the variable is defined for this environment and that protected
     variables are not used on an unprotected branch.
   - **Cache or artifact** — check the cache key and the `needs:`/`dependencies:` list.
   - **Runner** — check `tags:` against the available runners; a job stuck in `pending` has no matching runner.
   - **Flaky test** — rerun once. If it passes, open an issue for the flaky test; do not add `retry:` to hide it.
4. Fix the cause in the repository and push. Do not change the job to `allow_failure: true` to make the
   pipeline green.

## 5. Done

- The lint passes and a pipeline on the branch is green.
- The merge request description names the jobs that changed and why.

workflows.name: release-pipeline
workflows.description: Build or fix a CI/CD pipeline that tests, builds, and releases a service through gated environments.
workflows.use_when: The request asks to create, fix, speed up or harden a GitLab CI or GitHub Actions pipeline, or to set up build, release and deploy jobs for a service.
workflows.avoid_when: The request is a security scan of existing code or images only; use the security scan workflow.

steps.title: Read the current pipeline
steps.do: open `.gitlab-ci.yml` (and its `include:` files) or `.github/workflows/*.yml`. List stages, jobs, triggers, runners, and the last failed job log (`glab ci view`, `gh run view --log-failed`).
steps.done_when: you can describe the current flow from commit to release and name what is missing or failing.

steps.title: Change the pipeline
steps.do: follow `gitlab-ci-patterns` for GitLab or `github-actions-patterns` for GitHub. Keep the order lint → test → build → scan → release → deploy. Build the artifact once and promote the same digest to every environment. Ask the user first before you change a deploy job that targets production.
steps.done_when: the config passes the linter (`glab ci lint`, `actionlint`) and every job has a timeout.

steps.title: Gate the release
steps.do: add a protected manual or approval gate before production, and a rollback job or documented rollback command. Ask the user first before you run any deploy job or change protected environment settings.
steps.done_when: a production deploy cannot start without the gate and green test, build, and scan jobs.

steps.title: Prove it on a branch
steps.do: push to a feature branch and run the pipeline up to the last non-production stage. Fix each failure from its job log. Ask the user first if a job could reach a shared or production environment.
steps.done_when: the branch pipeline is green up to staging, and the docs page of the pipeline lists stages, gates, variables, and the rollback command.

areas.summary: Operating production databases: access roles, backups, and safe migration runs.

rules.name: access-control
rules.description: Least-privilege database roles, credentials, pooling, and audit settings for service databases.
rules.body:
- Create one `app_<service>` role per service with only `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` on its own tables.
- Create a separate `migration_<service>` role for DDL; never grant `CREATE`, `ALTER`, or `DROP` to the application role.
- Create `readonly_<service>` roles with `SELECT` only for reporting and support access.
- Never use `GRANT ALL` or grant `SUPERUSER` to an application or migration role.
- Store each service credential in a secret manager (Vault, cloud secret store); never share one password between services.
- Rotate database credentials at least every 90 days and after offboarding a person with database access.
- Connect applications through a connection pooler (`pgbouncer` in transaction mode) and set a pool size limit per service.
- Enable `pgaudit` (or the engine equivalent) for all DDL and role changes.
- Revoke `CREATE` on schema `public` from `PUBLIC` and put service tables in a named schema.
- Require TLS (`sslmode=verify-full`) in every client connection string.

rules.name: backup-policy
rules.description: Backup schedule, retention, encryption, restore tests, and alerts for production databases.
rules.body:
- Enable continuous WAL archiving to object storage for point-in-time recovery of every production PostgreSQL database.
- Run a daily full backup in addition to WAL archiving.
- Keep WAL for 7 days, daily backups for 30 days, weekly backups for 3 months, and monthly backups for 1 year.
- Take a snapshot before every production migration and keep it until the next major release.
- Encrypt every backup at rest with KMS-managed keys (AES-256).
- Store backups in a different account or project than the database and enable object lock or versioning.
- Run a restore test into an isolated environment every week and record the restore time and a row-count check.
- Set RTO 30 min and RPO 15 min for tier 1 databases; set RTO 4 h and RPO 1 h for tier 2.
- Alert when no backup completed in the last 26 hours.
- Alert when a backup size differs from the 7-day average by more than 20 %.
- Alert when backup storage use exceeds 70 % of its quota.

rules.name: migration-runbook
rules.description: Safety checks for running schema migrations against production databases.
rules.body:
- Use expand-and-contract for breaking schema changes: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, then remove the old column in a later release.
- Never rename or drop a column that the running application version still reads.
- Keep every migration compatible with the application version that runs before and after the deploy.
- Run the migration on staging with production-size data and record the execution time in the merge request.
- Take and verify a backup snapshot before running a production migration.
- Prepare and test the rollback SQL (or the down migration) before the production run.
- Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on PostgreSQL tables over 1 million rows.
- Do not add a `NOT NULL` column with a volatile default to a large table in one statement; add it nullable, backfill, then add the constraint.
- Set `lock_timeout` (for example `SET lock_timeout = '5s'`) and `statement_timeout` in the migration session.
- Backfill data in batches of at most 10,000 rows with a pause between batches.
- Run migrations with the `migration_<service>` role from the CI job, not from a developer machine.
- Announce a maintenance window when the expected lock time exceeds 5 minutes.

skills.name: backup-restore
skills.description: Procedure to verify a PostgreSQL or MySQL backup by restoring it into a scratch instance, and to run a point-in-time restore. Use when you check backups, set up backup jobs, or must restore data.
skills.body:
A backup counts only after a restore from it succeeds. Work on a scratch instance unless the user asks for a
production restore.

## 1. Find the backup setup

1. Find the backup tool and schedule: `pgbackrest`, `wal-g`, `barman`, `pg_dump` cron jobs, a Kubernetes
   operator (CloudNativePG, Zalando), or a managed service snapshot.
2. Record the retention, the WAL or binlog archive location, and the encryption key location.
3. If no backup job exists, stop and tell the user. Do not create one without agreement on the storage target.

## 2. List the latest backups

```bash
pgbackrest --stanza=<name> info
wal-g backup-list --detail
aws rds describe-db-snapshots --db-instance-identifier <id> --query 'DBSnapshots[-3:]'
```

Check that the newest full backup is younger than the policy allows and that WAL archiving has no gap.

## 3. Restore into a scratch instance

1. Start an empty instance with the same major version as the source:
   `docker run -d --name restore-check -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=check postgres:<major>`.
2. Restore the latest backup:
   - `pg_dump` custom format: `pg_restore --no-owner --dbname=<scratch-url> <file>.dump`.
   - pgBackRest: `pgbackrest --stanza=<name> --pg1-path=<scratch-data-dir> restore`.
   - WAL-G: `wal-g backup-fetch <scratch-data-dir> LATEST`, then start the server with recovery settings.
   - Managed service: restore the snapshot to a new instance name with a `restore-check-` prefix.
3. Time the restore. Compare it with the recovery time objective (RTO).

## 4. Check the restored data

1. Compare row counts of the largest tables with the source, within the backup age:
   `SELECT relname, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_live_tup DESC LIMIT 10;`
2. Read the newest timestamp of a write-heavy table. The gap to the backup time is the real recovery point
   (RPO).
3. Run `SELECT count(*)` on one table per schema to force a full read of its pages.
4. If counts or timestamps are off, the backup fails. Report the gap and keep the scratch instance for analysis.

## 5. Point-in-time restore (incident)

1. Ask the user first: confirm the target time, the target instance, and that writes to it are stopped.
2. Restore to a new instance, never over the damaged one:
   `pgbackrest --stanza=<name> --type=time --target="<YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS+00>" restore`.
3. Check the data with step 4 and let the user confirm before traffic moves.
4. Ask the user first before you switch the application connection string or copy rows back.

## 6. Clean up

- Delete the scratch instance and any restored snapshot copy.
- Record the restore duration, the measured RPO, and the backup id in the docs page of the database service.

areas.summary: Security checks in the delivery path: container hardening, scan gates, and admission policies.

rules.name: container-security
rules.description: Hardening requirements for Dockerfiles and container images of backend services.
rules.body:
- Pin every `FROM` image by `@sha256` digest; never use `:latest` or a tag-only reference.
- Use a multi-stage build and copy only the built artifact into the runtime stage.
- Use a minimal runtime base image (`distroless`, `-slim`, or Alpine); do not ship compilers or package managers in the runtime stage.
- Set `USER` to a numeric non-root UID (for example `USER 1000:1000`) in the final stage.
- Never `COPY` a `.env` file or pass a secret through `ARG` or `ENV`; use BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` for build secrets.
- Add `.env`, `.git`, and credential files to `.dockerignore`.
- Remove SETUID and SETGID bits in the runtime stage (`find / -perm /6000 -type f -exec chmod a-s {} +`).
- Use the exec form of `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` so the process receives `SIGTERM`.
- Run `trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1` on every built image in CI.
- Record every `.trivyignore` entry with the CVE id, the reason, a ticket reference, and a review date.
- Keep the image writable only under mounted paths so it runs with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`.

rules.name: policy-as-code
rules.description: Admission policies (Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper) that every cluster enforces, and how to test them.
rules.body:
- Keep admission policies in the repository under `policies/`; do not create policies by hand in a cluster.
- Enforce these policies in every cluster: `disallow-privileged-containers`, `require-non-root-user`, `require-resource-limits`, `require-image-digest`, `disallow-host-namespaces`.
- Set `require-readonly-root-filesystem` to `Audit` in staging and `Enforce` in production.
- Require verified image signatures (`verifyImages` in Kyverno or an equivalent constraint) in production namespaces.
- Use Kyverno YAML policies for single-resource checks; use OPA Rego only when a policy needs cross-resource data.
- Add a test case for each policy: `kyverno test .` with pass and fail resources, or `opa test policies/ -v` for Rego.
- Run the policy tests in CI and fail the pipeline on any failed test case.
- Roll out a new policy with `validationFailureAction: Audit` first and switch to `Enforce` after the audit report shows no violations.
- Limit a `PolicyException` to named resources and set an expiry date annotation on it.

rules.name: shift-left-policy
rules.description: Security scan jobs that CI must run, their severity thresholds, and the fix deadlines per severity.
rules.body:
- Run a secret scan (`gitleaks` or `trufflehog`) in a pre-commit hook and in CI on every merge request.
- Run SAST (`semgrep` or the GitLab SAST template) in CI on every merge request.
- Run a dependency scan (`trivy fs .`, `osv-scanner`, or the ecosystem audit command) before the build job.
- Run `trivy image` on the built image before it is pushed to a release registry.
- Run `syft` to create an SBOM for every release image and attach it with `cosign attest`.
- Run `cosign verify` on the image in the deploy job before rollout.
- Fail the merge request pipeline and the deploy job on any `Critical` or `High` finding.
- Post `Medium` findings as a merge request comment; do not block on `Medium` or `Low` findings.
- Set the fix deadline for `Critical` findings (CVSS 9.0–10.0) to the same day.
- Set the fix deadline for `High` findings (CVSS 7.0–8.9) to 72 hours.
- Create a ticket with a 2-week deadline for every `Medium` finding (CVSS 4.0–6.9).
- Document every exception in the scanner ignore file with a reason, a ticket, an owner, and an expiry of at most 30 days.
- Add an inline suppression with a reason for every SAST false positive; never disable a scanner rule globally for one finding.

skills.name: sbom-supply-chain
skills.description: Procedure to generate an SBOM, scan it for vulnerabilities, and sign and verify container images and attestations with cosign. Use when you add SBOM, image signing, or provenance to a pipeline or verify an image.
skills.body:
## 1. Generate the SBOM from the built image

Build the image once and refer to it by digest in every later step.

```bash
IMAGE=registry.example.com/group/service@sha256:<digest>
syft "$IMAGE" -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json
```

- Use the image, not the source tree, so the SBOM lists what ships.
- Keep `sbom.cdx.json` as a pipeline artifact (`artifacts:` in GitLab, `actions/upload-artifact` in GitHub).

## 2. Scan the SBOM

```bash
grype sbom:sbom.cdx.json --fail-on high
trivy sbom sbom.cdx.json --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1
```

1. If a finding has a fixed version, upgrade the package or the base image and rebuild.
2. If there is no fix, decide with the user: accept with an expiry date in the ignore file
   (`.grype.yaml` or `.trivyignore`) and a reason comment, or block the release.
3. Do not raise `--fail-on` to make the job pass.

## 3. Sign the image

Prefer keyless signing with the pipeline OIDC identity.

- GitLab: add `id_tokens: SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN: aud: sigstore` to the job.
- GitHub: set `permissions: id-token: write`.

```bash
cosign sign --yes "$IMAGE"
cosign attest --yes --type cyclonedx --predicate sbom.cdx.json "$IMAGE"
```

If the project uses a key pair, read it from a KMS (`--key gcpkms://...`, `awskms://...`, `hashivault://...`).
Never commit `cosign.key`.

## 4. Verify before deploy

```bash
cosign verify "$IMAGE" \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://gitlab.example.com/group/service//' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://gitlab.example.com
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx "$IMAGE" ...same identity flags...
```

1. Add the verify step to the deploy job, before the deploy command.
2. In Kubernetes, enforce the same identity with an admission policy (Kyverno `verifyImages` or Sigstore
   policy-controller). Ask the user first before you enable enforcement on a production cluster.

## 5. Done

- The pipeline produces the SBOM, fails on high and critical findings, and signs the image by digest.
- The deploy job verifies the signature and stops on a failed verification.

skills.name: secret-detection
skills.description: Procedure to scan a repository and its history for secrets with gitleaks, triage hits, rotate a leaked secret, and add the scan to pre-commit and CI. Use when a secret leaks or when you set up secret scanning.
skills.body:
## 1. Scan

```bash
gitleaks dir . --redact --report-format json --report-path /tmp/gitleaks.json   # working tree
gitleaks git . --redact --log-opts="--all"                                       # full history
```

Use `--redact` so the output does not print the secret again.

## 2. Triage each hit

1. Open the file and line. Decide: real secret, test fixture, or false positive.
2. A test fixture or false positive goes into `.gitleaks.toml` as an allowlist entry with a path or a regex and
   a comment with the reason. Do not allowlist a whole directory of source code.
3. A real secret is a leak, even if the branch was never merged. Go to step 3.

## 3. Respond to a real leak

1. Tell the user at once: which secret, where, and since which commit.
2. Rotate first. Ask the user first, because revoking the old value can break running services. Create the
   new value in the secret store, deploy it, then revoke the old one.
3. Check the provider audit log for use of the old value between the leak commit and the revocation.
4. Remove the value from the code and read it from the environment or the secret store.
5. Rewrite history only if the user asks: `git filter-repo --replace-text <file>` needs a force push and every
   clone to re-clone. Rotation is required either way; history rewrite does not undo the leak.

## 4. Prevent the next leak

1. Add the pre-commit hook:

```yaml
- repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
  rev: v8.21.2
  hooks:
    - id: gitleaks
```

2. Add a CI job that fails on a hit:
   - GitLab: include the `Jobs/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml` template, or run
     `gitleaks git . --redact --log-opts="$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_DIFF_BASE_SHA..HEAD"` in a job.
   - GitHub: run `gitleaks git . --redact` in a job, or enable push protection in the repository settings.
3. Add `.env` and key file patterns (`*.pem`, `*.key`) to `.gitignore`.

## 5. Done

- The full-history scan has no untriaged hits.
- Every real secret is rotated, and the old value is revoked.
- Pre-commit and CI run the scan.

workflows.name: security-scan
workflows.description: Scan code, dependencies, images, and IaC, triage the findings, and add the scans as pipeline gates.
workflows.use_when: The request asks to run or add SAST, secret, dependency, container image or IaC scans, to triage scanner findings, or to produce an SBOM or signed image.
workflows.avoid_when: Designing or building the release pipeline itself; use the release pipeline workflow.

steps.title: Run the scans
steps.do: run the scanners that match the scope from the repository root, with pinned versions: `semgrep scan --config auto`, `gitleaks detect --redact`, `trivy fs --severity HIGH,CRITICAL .`, `trivy image <image>@<digest>`, `checkov -d <iac-dir>`. Save machine output (`--format sarif` or `json`).
steps.done_when: each scanner exits and you have its findings count by severity.

steps.title: Triage
steps.do: for each `HIGH` or `CRITICAL` finding, check reachability and exposure and classify it: `fix-now`, `false-positive` (with evidence), or `accepted-risk` (with owner and expiry). For a leaked secret, follow `secret-detection`: rotate first, then remove.
steps.done_when: every high and critical finding has a class and a reason.

steps.title: Fix
steps.do: upgrade dependencies and base images, change code or IaC, and record each false positive in the scanner ignore file (`.semgrepignore`, `.trivyignore`, `.gitleaksignore`) with a reason and expiry.
steps.done_when: a re-run shows no unclassified `HIGH` or `CRITICAL` finding.

steps.title: Gate the pipeline
steps.do: add the scans as blocking jobs on merge requests, and add SBOM and image signing with `sbom-supply-chain`. Ask the user first before you change protected branch settings or production admission policies.
steps.done_when: a merge request with a new critical finding fails the pipeline, and the docs page lists the scanners, thresholds, and accepted risks.

examples: Add a pre-release security gate for payment-service v2.5.0: semgrep, trivy for the repo and the image, gitleaks, and checkov.

areas.summary: Infrastructure as code with Terraform and Ansible: modules, state, secrets, and drift.

rules.name: ansible-standards
rules.description: Role layout, idempotency, inventory, and test requirements for Ansible playbooks and roles.
rules.body:
- Keep each role in `roles/<name>/` with `tasks/main.yml`, `defaults/main.yml`, `handlers/main.yml`, and `meta/main.yml`.
- Put every overridable variable with a safe default in `defaults/main.yml`; put internal constants in `vars/main.yml`.
- Use fully qualified module names (`ansible.builtin.apt`, `ansible.builtin.template`).
- Write idempotent tasks: use `state:` modules instead of `command` or `shell`; add `creates:`, `removes:`, or `changed_when:` when `command` is unavoidable.
- Trigger service restarts through `notify:` handlers, not through unconditional restart tasks.
- Set `validate:` on `template` and `copy` tasks for config files that have a checker (`sshd -t -f %s`, `visudo -cf %s`).
- Name every task and play with `name:`.
- Keep one inventory directory per environment (`inventory/staging/`, `inventory/production/`); never mix hosts of two environments in one file.
- Use RFC 5737 addresses (`192.0.2.10`) or host names in examples; never commit real internal host addresses to a public repository.
- Pin collections and roles with exact versions in `requirements.yml`.
- Run `ansible-lint` and `ansible-playbook --syntax-check` in CI on every change.
- Test roles with `molecule test` and require a second converge run to report `changed=0`.
- Run every production playbook with `--check --diff` first and review the output before the real run.

rules.name: iac-standards
rules.description: Layout, version pinning, naming, tagging, and review checks for Terraform code.
rules.body:
- Keep reusable modules in `modules/<name>/` without environment-specific values; keep `environments/<env>/` for tfvars and backend config.
- Set `required_version` with an upper bound (for example `">= 1.9, < 2.0"`) in every root module.
- Pin every provider in `required_providers` with a `~>` constraint and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
- Pin module sources to a version tag (`?ref=v1.4.2` or `version = "1.4.2"`); never use `?ref=main` or a branch name.
- Name resources with the pattern `${var.project}-${var.environment}-${var.name}`.
- Add the tags `Project`, `Environment`, `ManagedBy = "terraform"`, `Owner`, and `CostCenter` to every taggable resource (use provider `default_tags` where available).
- Declare `type` and `description` for every variable and `description` for every output.
- Add `validation` blocks for variables with a closed set of values (environment names, sizes).
- Use `for_each` with stable keys instead of `count` for collections of named resources.
- Use `moved` blocks to rename or restructure resources instead of destroy and create.
- Set `prevent_destroy = true` in `lifecycle` for databases, state buckets, and KMS keys.
- Run `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate`, and `tflint` in CI on every change.
- Post the `terraform plan` output to the merge request and apply only the reviewed plan file (`terraform apply <planfile>`).
- Apply only from CI; never run `terraform apply` against staging or production from a workstation.

rules.name: immutability
rules.description: No in-place changes to running infrastructure, drift checks, and the emergency change path.
rules.body:
- Fix a running server with a new image and a redeploy; never patch it over SSH or in the cloud console.
- Change production resources only through Terraform code; do not use the console, CLI, or SDK for them.
- Build machine images with Packer (`*.pkr.hcl`) and reference them by image ID or digest, not by a `latest` name filter.
- Use `create_before_destroy = true` for resources that serve traffic during replacement.
- Run a scheduled drift check (`terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`) at least every 6 hours for each production state.
- Tag each drift finding `accept`, `remediate`, or `investigate`; fix a `remediate` finding within 48 hours.
- Create a P1 incident for drift of unknown origin and for any drift in security groups or IAM `policy` resources.
- Allow a manual production change only during a P0 incident and merge the matching IaC change within 24 hours.

rules.name: secret-hygiene
rules.description: Keep secrets out of Terraform and Ansible code, variables, and state.
rules.body:
- Never write a password, token, or private key as a literal in a `.tf`, `.tfvars`, or Ansible vars file.
- Read secrets at apply time from a secret manager data source (`aws_secretsmanager_secret_version`, `vault_kv_secret_v2`, `google_secret_manager_secret_version`).
- Prefer generated secrets (`random_password`) written straight to the secret manager over values passed in variables.
- Set `sensitive = true` on every variable and output that holds a secret; never override it to `false`.
- Encrypt Ansible secrets with `ansible-vault` or look them up from Vault; never commit plain-text secrets in `group_vars/` or `host_vars/`.
- Inject runtime secrets into Kubernetes with External Secrets Operator or a CSI secret driver; do not set them as Terraform string literals in pod env.
- Add a `gitleaks` or `trufflehog` pre-commit hook and CI job to every infrastructure repository.
- Rotate a leaked secret first, then remove it from Git history with `git filter-repo`, then check the access logs for its use.

rules.name: state-management
rules.description: Remote backend, isolation, locking, protection, and safe state operations for Terraform state.
rules.body:
- Use a remote backend (`s3`, `gcs`, `azurerm`, or HCP Terraform) for every non-local environment.
- Keep one state per `environment/component` key; never share a state between staging and production.
- Use separate buckets (or accounts) for staging and production state.
- Enable state locking (`use_lockfile = true` or `dynamodb_table` for S3; built-in for GCS) and never disable it.
- Enable versioning, encryption with a KMS key (`encrypt = true`, `kms_key_id`), and a public access block on the state bucket.
- Limit state bucket access to CI roles and on-call engineers with MFA.
- Do not read `terraform_remote_state` across environment boundaries; publish shared values to SSM Parameter Store or another key-value store.
- Use `import` blocks (Terraform 1.5+) to adopt existing resources and require `terraform plan` to show no changes after import.
- Prefer `moved` blocks over `terraform state mv`; run `terraform state pull > backup-<date>.tfstate` before any `state mv` or `state rm`.
- Run `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only after you confirm that no apply job holds the lock.
- Never delete old state versions from the bucket by hand.

skills.name: drift-detection
skills.description: Procedure to detect and resolve drift between Terraform/OpenTofu code, state, and real infrastructure with plan -detailed-exitcode, import, and refresh-only. Use when a plan shows unexpected changes or when you set up scheduled drift checks.
skills.body:
Drift means the real resources differ from the code. Resolve it in code; do not hide it.

## 1. Detect

```bash
terraform init -input=false
terraform plan -input=false -lock=false -detailed-exitcode -out=drift.tfplan
echo $?   # 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes (drift or unapplied code)
terraform show -no-color drift.tfplan > drift.txt
```

Use `tofu` instead of `terraform` if the project uses OpenTofu. Run against every environment directory or
workspace that the task names.

## 2. Classify each changed resource

Read `drift.txt` and sort every resource into one class:

1. **Unapplied code** — the code changed on the default branch but nobody applied it. Check `git log` for the
   module. Resolution: apply through the normal pipeline.
2. **Manual change** — someone changed the resource in the console or with a CLI. Check the cloud audit log
   (CloudTrail, GCP Audit Logs, Azure Activity Log) for the actor and time.
3. **Provider-side default** — the provider or service sets a value the code does not set, and the plan shows it
   on every run. Resolution: set the value in code, or add the attribute to `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] }`
   with a comment that names the reason.
4. **Resource outside state** — the resource exists but state does not track it.

## 3. Resolve

- Manual change that must stay: copy the value into the code, then run `plan` again until it shows no change.
- Manual change that must go: keep the code. The next apply reverts it. Ask the user first before that apply.
- Resource outside state: add an `import` block and plan:

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.logs
  id = "group-service-logs"
}
```

- Changed outputs or data sources only: run `terraform apply -refresh-only` to update state. Ask the user first;
  it writes state.
- Never run `terraform state rm` to make drift disappear unless the user wants to stop managing the resource.

## 4. Verify

1. Run step 1 again. The exit code must be `0`, or every remaining change must be a planned code change.
2. Commit the code changes with the drift cause in the commit body.

## 5. Schedule the check (optional)

- GitLab: a scheduled pipeline job runs step 1 and fails on exit code `2`. Use a read-only cloud role.
- GitHub: a workflow with `on: schedule` runs the same job with OIDC credentials for a read-only role.
- Send the failure to the team channel or open an issue with `drift.txt` attached. Do not apply from the
  scheduled job.

skills.name: terraform-modules
skills.description: Procedure to create or change a Terraform/OpenTofu module: inputs and outputs, version pins, fmt/validate/tflint/test, and safe renames with moved blocks. Use when you edit *.tf files of a module or move resources between modules.
skills.body:
## 1. Read the module and its callers

1. Open `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `versions.tf`, and `main.tf` of the module.
2. Find every caller: `grep -rn 'source *= *".*<module-name>' --include=*.tf .`
3. If the module is published with a version (registry or git tag), check which versions the callers pin.

## 2. Change the interface

1. Give every new variable a `type`, a `description`, and a `validation` block when the value has a fixed form.
2. Give a new variable a `default` only if every caller can use it. A variable without a default is a breaking
   change for callers.
3. Mark secrets `sensitive = true` in variables and outputs.
4. Do not rename or delete a variable or an output that a caller uses. Add the new one, keep the old one with a
   deprecation note in its `description`, and remove it in a later major version.
5. Pin providers in `versions.tf` with `required_providers` and a `~>` constraint, and set `required_version`.

## 3. Rename or move resources without destroy

A changed resource address makes Terraform destroy and recreate the resource. Add a `moved` block instead:

```hcl
moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.this
  to   = aws_s3_bucket.logs
}
```

- Moving a resource into a child module: `from = aws_s3_bucket.logs`, `to = module.logs.aws_s3_bucket.this`.
- Moving between state files needs `terraform state mv` or `removed` + `import` blocks. Ask the user first; it
  writes state.

## 4. Check

```bash
terraform fmt -recursive -check
terraform init -backend=false && terraform validate
tflint --recursive
terraform test            # if the module has tests/*.tftest.hcl
```

1. Add or update a `tests/<name>.tftest.hcl` with `command = plan` for each new input combination.
2. Run `terraform plan` in one caller environment. The plan must show no `destroy` or `forces replacement` line
   that the task did not ask for. Look for `# forces replacement` in the output.
3. If the plan replaces a stateful resource (database, bucket, volume), stop and tell the user.

## 5. Release

1. Update the module `README.md` inputs and outputs table (`terraform-docs markdown table . > README.md` if the
   project uses terraform-docs).
2. If the module is versioned, bump the major version for a breaking interface change, the minor version for a
   new input or output.
3. Applying the change to an environment goes through the pipeline. Ask the user first before any
   `terraform apply`.

areas.summary: Kubernetes clusters and workloads: manifests, Helm charts, resources, security, and upgrades.

rules.name: cluster-standards
rules.description: Control plane, node, runtime, CNI, and exposure standards for Kubernetes clusters and their config.
rules.body:
- Run at least 3 control plane nodes across 3 failure domains in production; allow a single control plane node only in clusters labelled `env=dev`.
- Never schedule etcd on worker nodes.
- Use a managed control plane (EKS, GKE, AKS) or kubeadm, RKE2, k3s, or Talos for self-managed clusters.
- Use `containerd` as the container runtime; never use Docker Engine as the CRI.
- Keep the same OS image and kernel version within a node group.
- Add the labels `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, `topology.kubernetes.io/region`, `node.kubernetes.io/instance-type`, and `environment` to every node.
- Use Cilium for new clusters; use Calico only for existing clusters; never use Flannel outside dev clusters.
- Choose pod and service CIDR ranges that do not overlap each other or the routed network.
- Expose production services through `Ingress`, `Gateway`, or `type: LoadBalancer`; do not use `NodePort` in production.
- Enable etcd encryption at rest with an `EncryptionConfiguration` that uses a KMS or `aescbc` provider.
- Enable API server audit logging and ship the audit log to central storage.

rules.name: resource-governance
rules.description: Resource requests and limits, probes, autoscaling, disruption budgets, and quotas for Kubernetes workloads.
rules.body:
- Set `resources.requests.cpu`, `resources.requests.memory`, and `resources.limits.memory` for every container.
- Set `limits.memory` equal to `requests.memory` for stateful and tier 1 workloads (`Guaranteed` QoS for memory).
- Never deploy a `BestEffort` pod (no resources block) to a production namespace.
- Derive requests from observed usage: set CPU requests near the p95 of `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` rate and memory requests near the p95 working set plus 20 %.
- Add `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe` to every serving container; add `startupProbe` when start takes over 30 seconds.
- Do not point `livenessProbe` at an endpoint that checks downstream dependencies.
- Add a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` with `minReplicas: 2` or more for tier 1 stateless workloads.
- Do not set a fixed `replicas` value in the manifest when an HPA manages the deployment.
- Add a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable` for every workload with 2 or more replicas.
- Add `topologySpreadConstraints` on `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` with `maxSkew: 1` for tier 1 workloads.
- Add a `LimitRange` with default requests and limits to every production namespace.
- Add a `ResourceQuota` to every production namespace.
- Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` longer than the longest request timeout of the service.

rules.name: upgrade-policy
rules.description: Version skew limits, cadence, pre-checks, and order for Kubernetes cluster upgrades.
rules.body:
- Keep production clusters within 2 minor versions of the latest stable Kubernetes release.
- Apply patch versions to every cluster within 30 days of release.
- Upgrade one minor version at a time; never skip a minor version.
- Upgrade dev and staging first; upgrade production within 60 days after the staging upgrade passed.
- Keep nodes at most 2 minor versions behind the control plane, and never run `kubelet` newer than `kube-apiserver`.
- Keep `kubectl` within one minor version of the server.
- Check that cert-manager, the ingress controller, the CNI, and the GitOps controller list the target version as supported before the upgrade.
- Run `kubent` or `pluto detect-all-in-cluster` and remove every deprecated API before the upgrade.
- Take and verify an etcd snapshot within 1 hour before a self-managed control plane upgrade.
- Check that every node is `Ready` and that no `PodDisruptionBudget` blocks a drain (`ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` above 0).
- Do not start an upgrade during an open P0 or P1 incident.
- Upgrade the control plane before the nodes, one control plane node at a time.
- Upgrade worker nodes with `kubectl cordon`, `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data`, upgrade, and `kubectl uncordon`.
- Write the rollback steps (etcd snapshot restore, previous node image) in the upgrade merge request before you start.

rules.name: workload-security
rules.description: Pod security, service accounts, RBAC, network policies, and secrets for Kubernetes workloads.
rules.body:
- Pin container images in production manifests by `@sha256` digest; never use the `latest` tag.
- Label production namespaces `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` and staging namespaces `enforce: baseline`.
- Set `runAsNonRoot: true`, a non-zero `runAsUser`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, and `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` on every container.
- Mount an `emptyDir` volume for paths the application writes, such as `/tmp`.
- Never set `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, or `hostIPC` in a workload namespace.
- Create a dedicated `ServiceAccount` per workload; never use the `default` service account.
- Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` unless the pod calls the Kubernetes API.
- Use a namespaced `Role` and `RoleBinding`; use a `ClusterRole` only for cross-namespace access and document the reason in an annotation.
- Never bind `cluster-admin` or the `system:masters` group to an application identity.
- Do not use wildcard `*` in `verbs`, `resources`, or `apiGroups` of a Role or ClusterRole.
- Check every new Role with `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>`.
- Add a `default-deny-all` NetworkPolicy (`podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]`) to every namespace.
- Allow egress to DNS (UDP and TCP port 53 to `kube-dns`) explicitly in namespaces with default deny.
- Allow ingress per workload with `podSelector` and `namespaceSelector` on labels; do not allow `0.0.0.0/0` ingress to pods.
- Never put secrets in a `ConfigMap` or as literal `env` values; sync them with External Secrets Operator from a secret manager.

skills.name: helm-charts
skills.description: Procedure to change a Helm chart: edit values and templates, lint, render, validate against the cluster schema, diff against the live release, and bump the chart version. Use when you edit files under charts/ or a Chart.yaml.
skills.body:
## 1. Read the chart

1. Open `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, and the templates the task touches.
2. Find the values files per environment (`values-<env>.yaml`, a helmfile, or an Argo CD / Flux manifest).
3. List chart dependencies: `helm dependency list charts/<name>`.

## 2. Make the change

1. Put every value that differs per environment in `values.yaml` with a safe default and a comment.
2. Use `required` for values without a safe default: `{{ required "image.tag is required" .Values.image.tag }}`.
3. Quote string values in templates: `{{ .Values.name | quote }}`.
4. Keep resources, probes, and security context configurable; do not hard-code them in a template.
5. If the chart has `values.schema.json`, add the new value to it.
6. Bump `version` in `Chart.yaml` for any chart change. Bump `appVersion` only when the default image changes.

## 3. Lint and render

```bash
helm dependency update charts/<name>
helm lint charts/<name> -f charts/<name>/values-<env>.yaml
helm template test charts/<name> -f charts/<name>/values-<env>.yaml > /tmp/rendered.yaml
kubeconform -strict -summary -kubernetes-version <cluster-version> /tmp/rendered.yaml
```

1. Render every environment values file, not only the default one.
2. Read the rendered output for the changed objects. Check names, labels, selectors, and image tags.
3. If the chart has unit tests (`helm unittest charts/<name>`), add a test for the change.

## 4. Diff against the live release

```bash
helm diff upgrade <release> charts/<name> -n <namespace> -f charts/<name>/values-<env>.yaml
```

1. This step reads the cluster. Ask the user first which context and namespace to use.
2. Check the diff for changes to immutable fields (`spec.selector`, `volumeClaimTemplates`). These fail the
   upgrade and need a delete and recreate; stop and tell the user.
3. Check that no Secret or PersistentVolumeClaim is deleted.

## 5. Release

1. If GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) deploys the chart, commit the change and let the controller sync it.
2. If the pipeline runs `helm upgrade`, it must use `--atomic --wait --timeout <n>m`.
3. Ask the user first before you run `helm upgrade`, `helm install`, or `helm rollback` against a cluster.
4. After the upgrade: `helm status <release> -n <namespace>` and `kubectl rollout status` for each changed
   workload.

skills.name: pod-troubleshooting
skills.description: Decision procedure to find why a Kubernetes pod is Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, ImagePullBackOff, not Ready, or unreachable, with read-only kubectl commands. Use when a workload does not start or does not serve traffic.
skills.body:
All commands in steps 1–4 are read-only. Confirm the context first: `kubectl config current-context`.

## 1. Get the state

```bash
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=<name> -o wide
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>          # read Events at the bottom
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
```

## 2. Follow the status

- **Pending**
  - Event `Insufficient cpu/memory`: requests are larger than free node capacity. Compare with
    `kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated`.
  - Event `didn't match node affinity/selector` or `untolerated taint`: check `nodeSelector`, `affinity`, and
    `tolerations`.
  - Event `unbound PersistentVolumeClaim`: `kubectl get pvc -n <ns>` and check the StorageClass.
- **ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull**
  - Check the image name and tag in the event. Check `imagePullSecrets` and that the registry allows the node.
- **CrashLoopBackOff**
  - Read the previous container log: `kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c <container> --previous`.
  - Exit code `1` or a stack trace: an application error; read config and env with
    `kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o yaml`.
  - Missing ConfigMap or Secret key: the event says `couldn't find key`.
- **OOMKilled** (`Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled`)
  - Compare `kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns>` with `resources.limits.memory`. For the JVM, check that
    `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` fits the limit. For Go, check `GOMEMLIMIT`.
- **Running but not Ready**
  - Read the readiness probe in `describe`. Run the probe from inside:
    `kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- wget -qO- localhost:<port><path>`.
- **Ready but unreachable**
  - `kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>` must list the pod IPs.
  - Compare the Service `selector` and `targetPort` with the pod labels and container port.
  - Check NetworkPolicies in the namespace: `kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>`.
  - Test from a debug pod: `kubectl debug -n <ns> -it <pod> --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- <svc>:<port>`.

## 3. Check recent changes

```bash
kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> -n <ns>
kubectl diff -f <manifest-or-rendered-chart>
```

Compare the failing revision with the last working one. A change in image, env, or config is the first suspect.

## 4. Write down the cause

State the cause with the event, log line, or metric that proves it.

## 5. Fix

1. Fix the cause in the manifest, chart values, or application code, and ship it through the normal pipeline.
2. Ask the user first before any change in the cluster: `kubectl rollout undo`, `kubectl delete pod`,
   `kubectl scale`, `kubectl edit`, or `helm rollback`.
3. After the fix: `kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> -n <ns>` returns success.

workflows.name: debug-workload
workflows.description: Diagnose a failing Kubernetes workload and fix it in the manifests or Helm values.
workflows.use_when: The request reports a pod in CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, failing probes, or a Service with no endpoints in Kubernetes.
workflows.avoid_when: The application code has a bug that reproduces outside the cluster; use the debug workflow.

steps.title: Read the state
steps.do: confirm the kube context with the user. Run read-only commands: `kubectl get pods -o wide`, `kubectl describe pod <pod>`, `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`, and `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`. Note the exit code, the reason, and the last good revision (`helm history <release>`).
steps.done_when: you can state the pod phase, the container reason, and the time it started.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.do: follow the `pod-troubleshooting` skill for the reason you found. Compare the failing revision with the last good one: image digest, values, ConfigMap, Secret keys, resources, probes (`helm diff revision <release> <good> <bad>` or `git diff`).
steps.done_when: one change or limit explains the failure, backed by an event, a log line, or a metric.

steps.title: Fix in source
steps.do: change the chart values, manifest, or application config in the repository, not with `kubectl edit`. Render and lint it (`helm template`, `helm lint`, `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` against a non-production cluster). Ask the user first before any command that writes to a cluster.
steps.done_when: the rendered manifest contains the fix and `helm lint` passes.

steps.title: Roll out and verify
steps.do: ask the user first before `helm upgrade`, `kubectl rollout restart`, or a rollback. After the user runs or approves it, watch `kubectl rollout status` and the restarts count.
steps.done_when: all replicas are `Ready`, restarts stay at 0 for 10 minutes, and the docs page of the service notes the cause.

examples: payment-service is in CrashLoopBackOff every 30 seconds since the v2.3.1 deploy; find the cause and fix it.

areas.summary: Network zones, ingress, and TLS for services and clusters.

rules.name: ingress-standards
rules.description: TLS, limits, timeouts, and CORS settings for Kubernetes Ingress and Gateway resources.
rules.body:
- Set `spec.ingressClassName` on every Ingress; do not rely on the default class annotation.
- Add a `tls` block with a cert-manager issued secret to every production Ingress; never expose a production route over plain HTTP.
- Enable the HTTP to HTTPS redirect (`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"` or an `HTTPRoute` redirect filter).
- Set rate limits on every public Ingress (for example `limit-rps: "100"` and `limit-connections: "20"`).
- Set `proxy-body-size` explicitly (default `"10m"`) and document any larger value in the manifest.
- Set `proxy-connect-timeout` and `proxy-read-timeout` explicitly (for example `"10"` and `"60"`).
- Set CORS origins to an explicit list; never allow `*` origins on a production host.
- Use one host per Ingress resource and name the resource after the host.
- Do not enable `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet` or `server-snippet` annotations.

rules.name: network-segmentation
rules.description: Network zones, subnet placement, and access paths for cloud and bare-metal networks defined as code.
rules.body:
- Define four zones in the network module: public (load balancers), application (nodes and app servers), data (databases, queues, object storage), management (CI runners, bastion, monitoring).
- Put Kubernetes nodes and application servers in private subnets; never set `associate_public_ip_address = true` on a node.
- Do not add a NAT gateway or any `0.0.0.0/0` egress route to data subnets.
- Allow inbound traffic to the data zone only from application zone security groups on the database or queue port.
- Allow SSH to servers only through a bastion host or VPN with MFA; never open port 22 to `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Use security group IDs (`source_security_group_id`) in rules instead of wide CIDR blocks.
- Limit egress of CI runners and nodes to the registries and APIs they need with an egress `policy` or firewall rule.
- Enable flow logs on every VPC or subnet in production.
- Use mTLS between services when a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) runs in the cluster; set `PeerAuthentication` to `STRICT`.

rules.name: tls-policy
rules.description: Protocol versions, certificate sources, renewal, and HSTS for TLS endpoints.
rules.body:
- Set the minimum protocol to TLS 1.2 on every listener and disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
- Enable TLS 1.3 on every listener that supports it.
- Issue certificates with cert-manager `Certificate` or Ingress annotations; do not commit certificate or key files.
- Use an ACME `ClusterIssuer` (Let's Encrypt) for public hosts and a Vault PKI or internal CA issuer for internal hosts.
- Use the DNS-01 solver for wildcard certificates.
- Set `renewBefore` so certificates renew with at least 30 days left.
- Add an alert on `certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds` for certificates that expire in less than 14 days.
- Add the `Strict-Transport-Security` header with `max-age` of at least `31536000` on every public HTTPS host.
- Terminate TLS at the ingress or load balancer and re-encrypt to the pod when the traffic crosses an untrusted network.

areas.summary: Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerts for production services.

rules.name: alerting-standards
rules.description: Required labels, severities, burn-rate alerts, and routing for Prometheus alert rules and Alertmanager config.
rules.body:
- Add `severity`, `service`, and `team` labels and a `runbook_url` annotation to every alert rule.
- Use only the severities `critical` (pages on-call), `warning` (team channel), and `info` (no notification).
- Page only on symptoms that users see (error rate, latency, availability); route cause alerts such as CPU or disk to `warning` or `info`.
- Define a fast-burn alert (1 h and 5 min windows, burn rate 14.4) and a slow-burn alert (6 h and 30 min windows, burn rate 6) for every SLO.
- Route fast-burn alerts as `critical` and slow-burn alerts as `warning`.
- Set a `for:` duration of at least `2m` on every alert that is not a burn-rate alert.
- Delete or rewrite an alert that fired 5 times in 30 days without a human action.
- Route alerts in Alertmanager by the `team` and `environment` labels; never page on-call for non-production alerts.
- Set `repeat_interval` and an escalation receiver for unacknowledged `critical` alerts.
- Add `inhibit_rules` so a cluster-wide or upstream alert suppresses the dependent service alerts.
- Create silences with an author, a comment, and an end time; never create a silence without an end time.
- Test every alert rule file with `promtool check rules` and `promtool test rules` in CI.
- Limit auto-remediation to reversible actions (restart a stateless pod) and emit an event for every automatic action.

rules.name: data-retention
rules.description: Retention, sampling, and cardinality limits for metrics, logs, and traces in the observability stack.
rules.body:
- Keep raw Prometheus metrics for 15 days and downsampled metrics in long-term storage (Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics) for 1 year.
- Keep logs hot for 30 days and in cold storage for 90 days, then delete them.
- Keep traces for 7 days and do not archive them.
- Never use `user_id`, `session_id`, `request_id`, or `trace_id` as a metric label.
- Limit each service to the series budget set in its scrape config with `sample_limit`.
- Drop unused high-cardinality series with `metric_relabel_configs` before ingestion.
- Sample `DEBUG` logs at 1 % in production and keep all `INFO`, `WARN`, and `ERROR` logs.
- Sample 10 % of traces at the head and keep every error trace and every trace slower than p99 with tail sampling.
- Use recording rules for queries that dashboards run on raw high-volume metrics.
- Redact secrets and personal data in the collector (`attributes` or `transform` processor) before export.

rules.name: golden-signals
rules.description: Golden-signal metrics, SLO coverage, and correlation that every production service exposes and dashboards show.
rules.body:
- Expose request rate, error rate, and latency histogram metrics for every endpoint or operation (for example `http_server_request_duration_seconds`).
- Expose saturation metrics: CPU, memory, connection pool use, and queue depth or worker concurrency.
- Label error metrics by class (`4xx`, `5xx`, or domain error code) and keep the label set bounded.
- Use histograms, not summaries, for latency so p50, p95, and p99 can be aggregated across pods.
- Add a `ServiceMonitor` or `PodMonitor` (or a scrape config) for every production service.
- Define at least one availability SLO and one latency SLO for every critical service and its main user journeys.
- Put one dashboard per service in the repository with panels for rate, errors, p99 latency, saturation, and SLO burn.
- Store dashboards as JSON or code (Grafonnet, Terraform) in the repository; do not edit production dashboards only in the UI.
- Propagate W3C `traceparent` across every service call and message.
- Write the `trace_id` into every log line so logs, metrics exemplars, and traces correlate.

skills.name: prometheus-alertmanager
skills.description: Procedure to add or change a Prometheus alerting or recording rule and its Alertmanager route, with promtool unit tests and amtool route checks. Use when you edit Prometheus rule files, PrometheusRule objects, or alertmanager.yml.
skills.body:
## 1. Find where rules live

1. Rule files (`*.rules.yml`, `rules/*.yml`) loaded by `rule_files:` in `prometheus.yml`, or `PrometheusRule`
   objects for the Prometheus Operator, or a Helm chart values block.
2. The Alertmanager config: `alertmanager.yml` or an `AlertmanagerConfig` object.
3. Existing alerts for the same service: reuse their labels (`severity`, `team`, `service`).

## 2. Write the query first

1. Run the expression in the Prometheus UI or with `promtool query instant <url> '<expr>'` against real data.
2. Alert on symptoms users see (error ratio, latency, saturation), not on every cause.
3. Use a ratio for errors: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))`.
4. If the query is expensive or reused, add a recording rule named `level:metric:operations`, for example
   `service:http_requests:rate5m`.

## 3. Write the rule

```yaml
- alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
  expr: service:http_errors:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout"} > 0.05
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "checkout 5xx ratio above 5% for 10m"
    runbook_url: "https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/checkout-errors"
```

- Set `for:` so one scrape spike does not page.
- Use only the severities that the Alertmanager routes know (for example `page`, `ticket`).
- Every paging alert has a `runbook_url`.

## 4. Test the rule

```bash
promtool check rules rules/checkout.rules.yml
promtool test rules tests/checkout.test.yml
```

Write a unit test with `input_series` that fires the alert and one that does not:

```yaml
rule_files: [../rules/checkout.rules.yml]
tests:
  - interval: 1m
    input_series:
      - series: 'service:http_errors:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout"}'
        values: '0.1x20'
    alert_rule_test:
      - eval_time: 15m
        alertname: CheckoutHighErrorRate
        exp_alerts: [{exp_labels: {severity: page, service: checkout}}]
```

## 5. Check the route

```bash
amtool check-config alertmanager.yml
amtool config routes test --config.file=alertmanager.yml severity=page service=checkout
```

The output must name the receiver you expect. If it names the default receiver, add a route.

## 6. Ship

1. Commit the rule, the test, and the route change together.
2. After the change reaches Prometheus, check `/rules` or `/api/v1/rules` for the rule state and errors.
3. Ask the user first before you reload a production Prometheus or Alertmanager by hand
   (`curl -X POST <url>/-/reload`).

skills.name: slo-implementation
skills.description: Procedure to define an SLO for a service and implement it in Prometheus: choose the SLI, write recording rules, and add multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts. Use when you add or change an SLO, an error budget, or burn-rate alerts.
skills.body:
## 1. Choose the SLI

1. Pick one user journey per SLO (for example "checkout API responds").
2. Choose the SLI type:
   - **Availability** — good events / valid events, for example non-5xx responses / all responses.
   - **Latency** — requests faster than a threshold / all requests, from a histogram bucket.
3. Measure as close to the user as the data allows: load balancer or ingress metrics before application
   metrics.
4. Exclude invalid events (health checks, 4xx caused by the client) in the label selector, and write down why.

## 2. Set the target

1. Read the last 4 weeks of the SLI. Set the target slightly below what the service achieves, not above it.
2. Use a 28-day or 30-day rolling window.
3. Compute the error budget: `1 - target`. A 99.9% target gives 43 minutes of full outage per 30 days.
4. Record the SLO in the service docs page: SLI query, target, window, owner.

## 3. Write recording rules

Record the error ratio for each alert window: 5m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 6h, 1d, 3d.

```yaml
- record: slo:sli_error:ratio_rate5m
  labels: {slo: checkout-availability}
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
    / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m]))
```

Repeat the rule per window (change only `[5m]` and the name). If the project uses Sloth or Pyrra, write the SLO
spec file instead and let the tool generate these rules.

## 4. Add burn-rate alerts

Use two windows per alert, so it fires fast and resets fast. For a 99.9% target (budget `0.001`):

| Severity | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget spent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| page | 1h | 5m | 14.4 | 2% |
| page | 6h | 30m | 6 | 5% |
| ticket | 3d | 6h | 1 | 10% |

```yaml
- alert: CheckoutAvailabilityBurnFast
  expr: |
    slo:sli_error:ratio_rate1h{slo="checkout-availability"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
    and slo:sli_error:ratio_rate5m{slo="checkout-availability"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
  labels: {severity: page}
```

## 5. Test and check

1. `promtool check rules <file>` and a `promtool test rules` case that fires the fast-burn alert.
2. Query the recording rules after deploy; each must return one series per SLO.
3. Add an SLO panel (SLI, target, remaining budget) to the service dashboard.

## 6. Use the budget

- Budget left: changes ship as usual.
- Budget spent in the window: write it into the service docs page and agree with the user which reliability
  work comes before new features. Do not lower the target to recover the budget.

areas.summary: Service reliability: SLOs and error budgets, on-call, and incident handling.

rules.name: on-call-standards
rules.description: Incident severities, response times, runbooks, access, and toil limits for on-call rotations.
rules.body:
- Use the severities P0 (full outage or data loss), P1 (major feature broken or over 25 % of users affected), P2 (degraded with a workaround), and P3 (no user impact).
- Acknowledge P0 pages within 5 minutes, P1 within 15 minutes, and P2 within 1 hour in business hours.
- Limit each engineer to 1 primary and 1 secondary on-call week per month.
- Link a runbook from every alert that can page; set an alert without a runbook to `warning` until the runbook exists.
- Store runbooks in the repository next to the alert rules or in `docs/runbooks/`.
- Give on-call engineers read access to production and write access limited to rollback, scale, and restart; require a separate MFA step for wider access.
- Document the escalation path in the paging tool and test it every quarter.
- Log every manual production action during an incident in the incident channel with a timestamp.
- Track toil hours per rotation; start automation work when toil exceeds 50 % of on-call time for 2 rotations in a row.

rules.name: slo-policy
rules.description: SLI and SLO definitions, targets per tier, and the error budget actions that gate releases.
rules.body:
- Define an SLI, an SLO target, and an error budget for every tier 1 service in an SLO file in the repository.
- Write each SLI as a ratio of good events to valid events (`good_requests / total_requests`), not as a raw average.
- Use availability and latency SLIs for HTTP and gRPC services, freshness or correctness SLIs for pipelines.
- Set tier 1 targets at 99.9 % (43 min budget per 28 days), tier 2 at 99.5 %, and tier 3 at 99.0 %.
- Use a 28-day rolling window for every SLO; do not use calendar months.
- Exclude only documented planned maintenance and synthetic traffic from the SLI query.
- Keep normal releases while more than 50 % of the budget remains.
- Add reliability tickets to the next iteration when 25–50 % of the budget remains.
- Stop feature releases and ship only reliability, security, and critical bug fixes when less than 25 % remains.
- Write an incident page and block feature releases until the budget recovers when the budget reaches 0 %.
- Record the approver and reason for every release made during a freeze in the release merge request.
- Review every SLO target each quarter against the measured reliability and update the SLO file.

skills.name: incident-command
skills.description: Procedure to run a production incident: declare and set severity, gather evidence, mitigate before root cause, keep a timeline, communicate, and hand off. Use when a service is down or degraded or an alert pages.
skills.body:
Mitigate first, find the root cause later. Every action on production needs the user's go-ahead.

## 1. Declare

1. State the symptom in one sentence: what fails, for whom, since when.
2. Set the severity from the project on-call rule (`on-call-standards.md` when the sre spec is installed):

| Severity | Condition |
|---|---|
| P0 | Full outage, data loss, or security breach |
| P1 | Major feature broken or over 25 % of users affected |
| P2 | Degraded with a workaround |
| P3 | No user impact yet |

3. Start a timeline with UTC times. Add every action and finding as one line.

## 2. Gather evidence (read-only)

1. Alerts and dashboards: error rate, latency, saturation of the service and its dependencies.
2. Recent changes: last deploys (`git log --since=<time>`, `kubectl rollout history`, pipeline history),
   feature flags, config changes, infrastructure changes.
3. Logs around the start time: filter by the error and by request id.
4. Dependencies: database, queue, external APIs, DNS, certificates (`openssl s_client -connect <host>:443`).
5. Write the leading hypothesis and the evidence for it.

## 3. Mitigate

Pick the smallest reversible action that stops the impact:

- Change shipped in the window → roll back the deploy or turn off the feature flag.
- Load spike → scale out or rate-limit.
- One bad instance or zone → drain it.
- Dependency down → fail over or degrade the feature.

Ask the user first before each action. Say the exact command, the expected effect, and how to undo it. After the
action, check the same metric that showed the symptom.

## 4. Communicate

1. P0/P1: post a status update every 30 minutes, even with no news: impact, current action, next update time.
2. State facts and the next step. Do not guess the root cause in public updates.

## 5. Resolve and hand off

1. Call the incident resolved when the symptom metric is back in its normal range for 15 minutes.
2. If you hand off to another person, pass the timeline, the current hypothesis, the actions taken, and open
   risks.
3. Write the incident page `docs/incidents/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<id>.md`: impact, root cause with evidence, fix with
   link and regression test, prevention actions with owners.

## 6. Find the root cause

1. Ask "why" from the symptom back to the defect until the answer is a change you can make in code, config,
   tests, alerts, or limits. "Human error" is not a root cause; ask why the system allowed it.
2. Add at least one prevention action: a test, an alert, a limit, or a rule.
3. Link the fix and its regression test in the incident page.

workflows.name: incident-response
workflows.description: Investigate an alert or production incident, mitigate it, fix the cause, and write the incident page.
workflows.use_when: The request reports a firing alert, an outage, elevated errors or latency, a database incident, or asks for a postmortem of a production event.
workflows.avoid_when: A bug found in development or tests with no production impact; use the debug workflow.

steps.title: Assess impact
steps.do: read the alert, the dashboard, and the SLO burn rate. Record what fails, for whom, and since when. Set the severity from `on-call-standards.md`. Read-only queries (logs, metrics, `kubectl get`, `describe`) are allowed; ask the user first before any command that changes production.
steps.done_when: the incident has a severity, a start time, and one sentence of user impact.

steps.title: Mitigate
steps.do: pick the fastest safe action from the evidence: roll back the last deploy, turn off a feature flag, scale out, fail over, or block bad traffic. Ask the user first and state the exact command before you run it.
steps.done_when: the error rate or latency is back under the SLO threshold for 15 minutes, or the user decides to stop mitigation.

steps.title: Find the root cause
steps.do: build a timeline from deploys, config changes, alerts, and logs. Test each hypothesis against data (queries, commits, traces) until one cause explains all symptoms. For a database incident, include slow queries, locks, replication lag, and connection counts. Use read-only access; ask the user first before a query that could load the production database.
steps.done_when: the cause is backed by evidence and is not "human error".

steps.title: Fix and prevent
steps.do: change the code, config, or alert that allowed the failure, with a regression test or a check. Add at least one prevention item (test, alert, limit, rule) with an owner. Ask the user first before you deploy it.
steps.done_when: the fix is in a change with green checks and each prevention item has an owner.

steps.title: Write the incident page
steps.do: write `docs/incidents/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<id>.md` with `covers:` for the changed code and the sections impact, root cause with evidence, fix with link and test, and prevention with owners.
steps.done_when: the page has all four sections and links the fix change.
